fuels.title: Classification of fuels
paragraphs: A fuel releases useful heat on combustion. By physical state: solid—wood, coal and charcoal; liquid—petroleum, petrol, diesel and kerosene; gaseous—natural gas, LPG, CNG, coal gas and water gas. LPG is stored as a pressurised liquid but used as a gaseous fuel.
Natural/primary fuels occur in nature, for example coal, crude petroleum and natural gas. Secondary/manufactured fuels are obtained by processing, for example coke, petrol and coal gas.

goodfuel.title: Characteristics of a good fuel
paragraphs: A good fuel has high calorific value, moderate ignition temperature, controllable combustion, low moisture and ash, and low smoke and harmful impurity content. It should be readily available, reasonably priced, easy and safe to store and transport, and should leave little corrosive residue.

Gaseous fuels mix readily with air, permit rapid starting/stopping and accurate flame control, normally leave negligible ash and need less manual handling. Their limitations are leakage/fire hazards and the need for pipelines or pressure-rated storage. Cost and calorific value cannot be ranked for all gases against all liquids or solids without specifying the fuel and comparison basis.

refining.title: Petroleum refining and fractional distillation
paragraphs: Petroleum is predominantly a mixture of alkanes, cycloalkanes (naphthenes) and aromatic hydrocarbons, with smaller amounts of sulphur-, nitrogen- and oxygen-containing compounds. Refining removes impurities and separates the crude into useful fractions of different boiling ranges.

Pretreatment: remove suspended solids by filtration; remove emulsified water by electrical coalescence (the course notes call this Cottrell treatment); remove objectionable sulphur compounds. The supplied historical example uses CuO, producing removable CuS. These are course descriptions, not a claim that every modern refinery uses the same treatment.

Heat the crude to about 400°C and feed it into the lower part of a fractionating column. The column is hot below and cooler above. Rising vapours repeatedly condense and vaporise on trays/bubble caps. High-boiling components condense lower down; low-boiling components reach higher levels. Withdraw each fraction at its appropriate level.

From top to bottom the notes list uncondensed gases, petroleum ether, gasoline (petrol), naphtha, kerosene, diesel and heavy oils. Further treatment/vacuum distillation of heavy material yields lubricating oils, waxes and heavy residues such as asphalt. Straight-run petrol is the gasoline obtained directly by this fractional distillation, before cracking or reforming.
Source qualification: the source uses “naphthalene” for cycloparaffins; the correct class name is naphthenes. Naphthalene itself is aromatic.

cracking.title: Cracking and the fluidized-bed catalytic process
paragraphs: Cracking is the conversion of heavy, high-boiling hydrocarbons into smaller hydrocarbons by heat, catalysts, or both. Example: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₅H₁₂ + C₅H₁₀. Thermal cracking includes liquid-phase and vapour-phase processes; catalytic cracking includes fixed-bed and fluidized-bed processes.

Preheat heavy oil, vaporise it and mix it with finely powdered silica–alumina/aluminosilicate catalyst. In the reactor, the gas suspends the particles as a fluidized bed; the course example operates near 500°C and 3–5 kg cm⁻². Heavy molecules crack to lighter products. A cyclone separates catalyst from the vapours, which go to a fractionating column for product recovery.

Coke deposited on the catalyst blocks active sites, reducing catalytic activity. Send spent catalyst to the regenerator and burn off coke in air (about 600°C in the supplied example). Return hot regenerated catalyst to fresh feed; its heat helps sustain cracking. The process improves gasoline yield/quality and supports continuous operation.

Source qualification: “fluidized bed” and “moving bed” are treated together in the question, but they are distinct reactor arrangements. This answer describes the fluidized powder/circulating-catalyst arrangement in the supplied notes. The deposit burned off is coke, not “coal embedded in catalyst”.

ft.title: Fischer–Tropsch synthetic fuel
paragraphs: Fischer–Tropsch synthesis converts purified synthesis gas (CO + H₂) to liquid hydrocarbons over cobalt- or iron-based catalysts. It provides liquid fuel from non-petroleum feedstocks such as coal, natural gas or biomass; its carbon footprint depends on feedstock and process energy.

In the historical course route, pass steam over red-hot coke to make water gas: C + H₂O → CO + H₂. Adjust the H₂:CO ratio for synthesis and remove sulphur compounds, which poison the catalyst. Compress the purified gas and pass it over catalyst at 200–300°C and 5–25 atm in the supplied example.

The notes specify 100 parts Co, 5 parts thoria, 8 parts magnesia and 200 parts kieselguhr. Cobalt is the active metal; thoria/magnesia are promoters and kieselguhr is a support. This historical formulation is not the only industrial catalyst.

Paraffins: nCO + (2n+1)H₂ → CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + nH₂O. Olefins: nCO + 2nH₂ → CₙH₂ₙ + nH₂O. Both represent exothermic synthesis. Cool the converter effluent, condense/separate liquids and fractionate them. Heavy products may be cracked; suitable unconverted gas may be recycled.

gasfuels.title: LPG, CNG and Hythane
paragraphs: LPG is mainly propane/butane obtained from petroleum refining and natural-gas processing. It is stored as a liquid under pressure; leaked vapour is heavier than air and can collect near the ground. Uses: cooking, heating and automotive/industrial fuel.

CNG is compressed natural gas, mainly methane (about 90–95% in the notes), supplied from natural-gas production/processing and associated petroleum gas. It is stored as gas at about 200–250 bar. It usually produces less particulate matter and CO₂ per unit energy than petrol/diesel; actual CO, NOₓ and methane emissions depend on the engine and operating conditions. High-pressure vessels and leak controls are essential.

Hythane is hydrogen-enriched CNG; the course blend is about 18–20% H₂ and 80–82% CNG by volume. Hydrogen can improve flame propagation and lean combustion and reduce carbon-containing emissions. It requires compatible equipment, and NOₓ reduction is not guaranteed.

Calorific values must use the same gross/net and mass/volume basis. Hydrogen enrichment raises mass-specific energy but lowers energy per normal gas volume compared with methane. LPG has convenient liquid storage; CNG is established for transport; Hythane is useful in suitably adapted low-emission fleets. There is no universally preferred fuel independent of cost, storage, infrastructure and safety requirements.

For a clearly stated illustrative lower-calorific-value comparison by mass: LPG ≈46 MJ kg⁻¹, methane-rich CNG ≈50 MJ kg⁻¹. Taking Hythane as 20 mol% H₂ and 80 mol% CH₄, H₂ mass fraction = (0.20×2)/(0.20×2+0.80×16) ≈0.0303. With LHV(H₂)≈120 and LHV(CH₄)≈50 MJ kg⁻¹, blend LHV≈0.0303×120+0.9697×50≈52.1 MJ kg⁻¹. These are general-chemistry illustrative values, not measured values supplied for a particular commercial fuel; do not compare them with gross or volume-based values.

hydrogen.title: Hydrogen production colours and green electrolysis
paragraphs: Hydrogen colours identify production routes, not different hydrogen molecules. Grey: fossil methane reforming without CO₂ capture; brown/black: coal gasification; blue: fossil-based production with carbon capture; turquoise: methane pyrolysis producing solid carbon; green: water electrolysis powered by renewable electricity. Capture efficiency and upstream emissions prevent blue hydrogen from being automatically zero-carbon.

The three electrolysers in the notes are alkaline, proton-exchange membrane (PEM) and solid-oxide. Direct current drives water splitting: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. Hydrogen forms at the cathode, oxygen at the anode; a separator prevents their mixing.
Alkaline (KOH/NaOH): cathode 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻; anode 2OH⁻ → ½O₂ + H₂O + 2e⁻. OH⁻ moves toward the anode.
PEM: anode H₂O → ½O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻; cathode 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Protons move through the membrane toward the cathode. Solid oxide: cathode H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + O²⁻; anode O²⁻ → ½O₂ + 2e⁻.

Renewable power is essential to the “green” label; electrolysis using fossil-generated electricity is not automatically green. Green hydrogen can help decarbonise fertilisers, refining and difficult-to-electrify industrial processes, subject to energy, cost and storage limitations.

batteryclasses.title: Battery classification
paragraphs: A battery converts stored chemical energy to electrical energy through redox reactions. Primary cells are intended for one discharge without recharging in normal service, for example dry cells and primary zinc–air cells. Secondary cells have reversible operating reactions and are recharged by an external electrical supply, for example lead–acid and lithium-ion batteries.

Reserve batteries keep an essential component separate until activation, giving long storage life; examples in the notes include magnesium–silver chloride systems. Fuel cells receive fuel and oxidant continuously from outside; a hydrogen–oxygen PEMFC continues supplying electricity while these reactants are supplied.

A battery normally stores active reactants internally and needs replacement or recharge after depletion. A fuel cell is refuelled, rather than recharged by reversing the entire stored-reactant inventory. Fuel cells give direct chemical-to-electrical conversion, quiet operation and useful efficiency; hydrogen–oxygen cells can also supply water in spacecraft. Their suitability still depends on reactant storage, system mass and reliability.

zincair.title: Zinc–air battery
paragraphs: Construction: zinc powder/gel is the negative electrode; a porous carbon/catalyst air electrode is the positive electrode. A separator prevents shorting. Aqueous KOH (about 30% in the supplied example) conducts ions, and gas-permeable layers admit atmospheric oxygen while managing electrolyte.

During discharge, zinc is oxidised and oxygen is reduced. A convenient balanced form is: anode Zn + 2OH⁻ → ZnO + H₂O + 2e⁻; cathode ½O₂ + H₂O + 2e⁻ → 2OH⁻. Overall: Zn + ½O₂ → ZnO. Electrons pass through the external load from zinc to the air electrode.

High energy density and low material cost follow partly from obtaining oxygen externally. Sealed shelf life is long, but life after opening the air seal and power capability are limited. Uses include hearing aids and small medical/portable devices. A standard primary hearing-aid zinc–air cell should not be assumed rechargeable; specialised rechargeable metal–air systems are different designs.

lithium.title: Secondary cell: lithium-ion battery
paragraphs: A lithium-ion cell shuttles Li⁺ reversibly between two intercalation electrodes. The supplied example uses graphite at the negative electrode, lithium cobalt oxide at the positive electrode, a separator and a non-aqueous lithium-salt electrolyte.

On discharge, the negative electrode releases lithium ions and electrons: LiC₆ → C₆ + Li⁺ + e⁻. The positive-electrode idealised reaction is CoO₂ + Li⁺ + e⁻ → LiCoO₂. Overall: LiC₆ + CoO₂ → C₆ + LiCoO₂. Li⁺ travels through the electrolyte and electrons through the external load toward the positive electrode.

Charging supplies external energy and reverses these transfers. The equations are idealised end-member bookkeeping; practical cells cycle over controlled partial states of charge, not complete conversion to pure CoO₂. Advantages include high energy density, relatively low self-discharge and long useful cycle life. Limitations include ageing, thermal-runaway risk and protection/charging requirements. Applications: phones, laptops, cameras, electric vehicles and storage.

“King of batteries” is an informal description of widespread use and favourable energy density, not a universal technical ranking. Source correction: the printed Li without a positive charge must be Li⁺; during discharge electrons and ions travel toward the same electrode through different paths, rather than in opposite directions.

sodium.title: Sodium-ion versus lithium-ion batteries
paragraphs: Sodium-ion cells store energy by reversible Na⁺ transfer. A representative cell uses a hard-carbon negative electrode, a sodium-containing transition-metal-oxide positive electrode and a sodium-salt electrolyte such as NaPF₆ in carbonate solvents. On discharge, sodium leaves the charged negative host, travels as Na⁺ through the electrolyte and inserts into the positive host; electrons flow through the load. Charging reverses the transfer.

Sodium is abundant and widely distributed, offering supply-security and possible cost advantages. Some designs permit aluminium current collectors on both electrodes and suit cost-sensitive stationary storage. Lithium-ion commonly uses graphite and Li-containing positive materials and has a mature manufacturing base and generally higher energy density in established commercial comparisons.

Larger/heavier Na⁺ and lower cell voltage can reduce gravimetric energy density, so sodium-ion is not automatically better for every portable or vehicle application. Safety, low-temperature behaviour, cycle life and cost depend on the specific chemistry and cell design; abundance alone does not guarantee a lower final battery price.

pem.title: Proton-exchange membrane fuel cell
paragraphs: Construction: two porous gas-diffusion electrodes with catalysts (commonly Pt), a proton-conducting polymer membrane between them, current collectors/flow channels and external load. Feed hydrogen to the anode and oxygen/air to the cathode.

Anode: 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. H⁺ crosses the membrane; electrons cannot pass through it and instead drive the external load. Cathode: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O. Overall: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, releasing electrical energy and heat. Remove product water and heat and maintain membrane hydration.

The membrane conducts protons, separates the reactant gases and blocks electronic short-circuiting. Relatively low operating temperature, quick startup, high power density and compact design favour automotive and portable applications. Applications also include backup power. Limitations include catalyst cost, hydrogen purity/storage, catalyst poisoning and water/thermal management.

coal.title: Coal analysis: proximate and ultimate
paragraphs: Anthracite is the highest-rank coal. Its calorific value varies with grade and reporting basis; the traditional course approximation is about 8,000–8,500 kcal kg⁻¹ (roughly 33–36 MJ kg⁻¹), rather than one universal measured value.

Proximate analysis: (1) Moisture—heat a known sample near 105–110°C to constant mass; moisture % = loss/original sample mass ×100. (2) Volatile matter—heat the dried sample in a covered crucible near 925°C for about 7 minutes under the specified test method; volatile % = additional loss/original mass ×100. Excluding air avoids burning the fixed carbon. (3) Ash—heat a separate known sample/open crucible in air near 700–750°C to constant residue; ash % = residue/original mass ×100. (4) Fixed carbon % = 100 − (moisture % + volatile % + ash %), all on the same reporting basis. Fixed carbon is not the same as total elemental carbon.

Moisture wastes heat in evaporation and increases handling weight. Volatile matter affects ignition, flame length, smoke and combustion-air/furnace design. Ash is non-combustible, reduces useful heat per mass and can cause slagging and disposal problems. High fixed carbon supports a sustained hot bed and is important in metallurgical coke. Low nitrogen reduces dilution and fuel-NOₓ potential. Sulphur can cause SOₓ pollution, corrosion and undesirable sulphur in metallurgical products; oxygen already bound in fuel generally lowers useful heating value.

Ultimate analysis reports elemental C, H, N, S and O (with ash/moisture basis stated). Burn a known sample in oxygen: C is calculated from collected CO₂, H from collected H₂O: %C = (12/44)(mass CO₂/sample mass)×100 and %H = (2/18)(mass H₂O/sample mass)×100. Determine N by an appropriate nitrogen-analysis method (the traditional course procedure is Kjeldahl), S by conversion to sulphate and BaSO₄ weighing: %S = (32/233)(mass BaSO₄/sample mass)×100. Oxygen is traditionally calculated by difference after accounting for all constituents on the stated basis. These results guide combustion-air calculation, calorific-value estimates and pollution control.

Kjeldahl working: digest a known coal mass with concentrated H₂SO₄ and the specified catalyst/salts; nitrogen is converted to ammonium species. Add excess NaOH, distil the liberated NH₃ into a known amount of standard acid and back-titrate the excess acid with a blank correction. For net V mL of acid of normality N consumed by NH₃ and m g coal, %N = 1.4VN/m. The balanced liberation step is (NH₄)₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O. The packet’s version omits one water molecule; this is an atom-balance correction. For its sulphur method, burn coal in oxygen in a bomb, extract sulphate in the washings/residue and precipitate with BaCl₂; Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄. Oxygen by difference must include ash/moisture corrections appropriate to the reporting basis; simply subtracting CHNS from 100 in an ash-containing sample overstates oxygen.

knocking.title: Knocking, octane and cetane numbers
paragraphs: In a spark-ignition petrol engine, knocking is rapid autoignition of the unburnt end-gas ahead of the normal flame, causing pressure waves and a metallic sound. It lowers smoothness/efficiency and can damage parts. Suitable high-octane fuel, correct ignition timing, cooling and appropriate compression ratio help prevent it. Diesel knock arises from excessive ignition delay followed by rapid combustion; do not confuse the two mechanisms.

Octane number measures resistance to knock in a standard spark-ignition test by comparison with iso-octane (100) and n-heptane (0). Cetane number measures ignition quality of diesel in a standard compression-ignition test; a higher value normally means a shorter ignition delay. It is not an efficiency rating of petrol. The historical reference pair is cetane (100) and α-methylnaphthalene (0); modern testing also uses calibrated reference fuels.

For the qualitative question comparing iso-octane, naphthalene and n-octane, aromatic naphthalene has high antiknock tendency and straight-chain n-octane knocks strongly; the conventional course ordering of increasing petrol knocking tendency is naphthalene < iso-octane < n-octane. This is a qualitative historical comparison, not a recommendation to blend solid naphthalene into fuel.

Tetraethyl lead (TEL) was historically added as an antiknock agent; it interferes with combustion-chain reactions. Ethylene dibromide was used as a lead scavenger, converting lead compounds to more volatile lead bromide and reducing deposits. The question’s “ethyl bromide” is historically imprecise: standard ethyl fluid used ethylene dibromide (often with ethylene dichloride). Leaded petrol and its scavengers are toxic legacy practice, not current fuel advice.

methanol.title: Methanol–oxygen fuel cell
paragraphs: A direct methanol cell electrochemically oxidises supplied methanol and reduces oxygen. In an acidic/proton-conducting description: anode CH₃OH + H₂O → CO₂ + 6H⁺ + 6e⁻; cathode 3/2 O₂ + 6H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 3H₂O. Overall CH₃OH + 3/2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Electrons pass through the load while ions move through the electrolyte.

The older alkaline form is equivalent: anode CH₃OH + 6OH⁻ → CO₂ + 5H₂O + 6e⁻; cathode 3/2 O₂ + 3H₂O + 6e⁻ → 6OH⁻. In an alkaline electrolyte, CO₂ can subsequently form carbonate. State which electrolyte convention is used rather than mixing half-reactions. Methanol is a convenient liquid fuel, but toxicity, crossover, catalyst cost and carbon emissions are limitations; it is distinct from the R25 hydrogen PEMFC.

solar.title: Solar cell
paragraphs: A solar cell converts light directly to electricity through the photovoltaic effect. In a semiconductor p–n junction, absorbed photons generate electron–hole pairs. The junction’s built-in electric field separates carriers, and contacts collect them to produce current through an external load. No fuel combustion is involved. Uses include rooftop/utility power, satellites, solar lighting, calculators and remote power supplies. Output depends on illumination, temperature and device efficiency; energy storage is needed for supply when sunlight is unavailable.

polymerisation.title: Polymerisation and its types
paragraphs: Polymerisation joins monomer molecules into macromolecules containing repeating units. In the course addition examples, unsaturated monomers add to a growing chain without loss of small molecules: nCH₂=CH₂ → [–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ; tetrafluoroethylene similarly forms PTFE.

Condensation polymerisation joins multifunctional monomers with elimination of small molecules such as water or HCl. A diamine plus a dicarboxylic acid gives polyamide links; phenol–formaldehyde condensation can form a cross-linked thermosetting network. Stepwise reactions first form oligomers and then higher-molar-mass chains/networks.

Copolymerisation uses two or more monomer species. Buna-S is a copolymer of styrene and 1,3-butadiene. Addition/condensation describes the reaction route; thermoplastic/thermoset describes thermal/network behaviour. A condensation polymer such as nylon can be thermoplastic, so the classifications must not be equated.

thermalpolymers.title: Thermoplastics and thermosets
paragraphs: Thermoplastics usually have linear/branched chains held together by intermolecular forces. They soften/melt on heating and can be reshaped within suitable processing limits; examples include PE, PVC, nylon and PTFE. Thermosets form a covalently cross-linked three-dimensional network during curing. Cured Bakelite/epoxy cannot simply be melted and remoulded; excessive heating causes degradation.

Networks restrict chain motion, often providing dimensional stability, rigidity and creep/heat resistance. Thermoplastics can often be reprocessed, whereas cured thermosets normally require other recycling routes. “Thermoplastics are weaker” is not a universal rule: strength depends on chemistry, reinforcement, orientation, temperature and the property measured.

Source correction: PTFE is an addition thermoplastic, not a thermoset. Its extremely high melt viscosity makes ordinary melt-flow processing difficult; it is commonly shaped by pressing/sintering or specialised methods. Difficult processing does not imply a covalently cross-linked thermoset network. Nylon is also a thermoplastic, despite its condensation synthesis.

ptfe.title: PTFE: preparation, properties and applications
paragraphs: Monomer: tetrafluoroethylene, CF₂=CF₂. Free-radical addition polymerisation under controlled pressure using an appropriate initiator gives nCF₂=CF₂ → [–CF₂–CF₂–]ₙ. The strong C–F bonds and shielding fluorine atoms contribute to chemical inertness and a low-energy non-stick surface.

Properties include chemical resistance, low friction, useful thermal resistance and excellent electrical insulation. PTFE is a thermoplastic with high melt viscosity. Uses: non-stick cookware coatings, chemical-resistant liners, gaskets/seals, bearings and wire/cable insulation. The source’s quoted high temperature is not a safe universal continuous-service rating; actual service limits are grade/design dependent.

Why it adheres to a pan: the coating is attached by engineered surface preparation and primer/binder systems, often with mechanical anchoring into a roughened/treated substrate, then cured/sintered. Its low surface adhesion to food does not imply that a specially engineered coating cannot be bonded to a substrate.

bunas.title: Buna-S: preparation, properties and applications
paragraphs: Monomers are 1,3-butadiene (CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂) and styrene (C₆H₅–CH=CH₂). Emulsion copolymerisation, traditionally about 75:25 butadiene:styrene in the supplied example with an initiator around 50°C, produces styrene–butadiene rubber (SBR/Buna-S). Conditions and microstructure vary by grade.

The butadiene-derived segments provide flexible, vulcanisable unsaturation; styrene units improve useful strength/abrasion behaviour. Vulcanisation introduces cross-links to improve elasticity and service performance. It has useful abrasion resistance and load-bearing properties, but can swell in organic solvents and suffer ozone attack. Uses: tyres, shoe soles, hoses, conveyor belts, gaskets and cable insulation.

kevlar.title: Kevlar: preparation, structure, properties and applications
paragraphs: Kevlar is an aromatic polyamide (aramid), poly(p-phenylene terephthalamide). Monomers for the practical condensation route are p-phenylenediamine, H₂N–C₆H₄–NH₂, and terephthaloyl chloride, ClCO–C₆H₄–COCl. They form [–NH–C₆H₄–NH–CO–C₆H₄–CO–]ₙ with elimination of HCl (chain ends neglected in the repeating-unit scheme).

The supplied simplified scheme uses terephthalic acid instead of the acid chloride and eliminates water; it identifies the same aromatic amide backbone but should not be mistaken for the industrial reaction conditions. Rigid para-linked aromatic chains, alignment and intermolecular hydrogen bonding give high tensile strength relative to mass.

Properties: high strength/stiffness, low density, heat/flame resistance and low electrical conductivity. UV exposure and some chemical environments can damage it. Uses: ballistic vests/helmets, ropes, cables, tyre reinforcement, aerospace/sporting composites and protective clothing. For the applications question: non-stick cookware—PTFE; shoe soles/tyres—Buna-S; body armour—Kevlar. The tyre material and body-armour material are different polymers, not one plastic.

conducting.title: Conducting polymers: classification, doping and uses
paragraphs: Conducting polymers carry charge through a conjugated polymer backbone or through conducting constituents in a composite. Intrinsic examples include polyacetylene, polyaniline and polypyrrole. Alternating/conjugated bonds permit delocalisation; doping creates additional mobile charge carriers. Oxidative (p-type) doping removes electrons, for example iodine treatment; reductive (n-type) doping adds electrons, for example with sodium naphthalenide.

Extrinsically conducting materials include polymers filled with carbon/metal particles and blends with conducting polymers. A connected conducting path forms above a composition-dependent percolation threshold. Conductivity depends on doping, structure, morphology and temperature; conjugation alone does not guarantee metal-like conduction.

Redox/doping changes can reversibly change optical absorption/colour, enabling electrochromic displays and optical filters. Other applications include antistatic coatings, sensors, flexible electronics, battery electrodes, corrosion-protection coatings and photovoltaic devices.

frp.title: Fibre-reinforced plastics
paragraphs: FRPs combine a polymer matrix (for example epoxy/polyester) with fibres such as glass, carbon or aramid. Fibres carry much of the directional load; the matrix binds and positions them, transfers stress and protects them from the environment. Reinforcement can be continuous/unidirectional, woven or chopped.

Glass FRP is relatively economical with useful strength and corrosion resistance; carbon FRP offers high specific stiffness/strength; aramid FRP offers low mass and useful impact resistance. Fibre orientation, fibre fraction and fibre–matrix bonding control performance.

Advantages: high strength/stiffness relative to mass, corrosion resistance, fatigue performance and freedom to form complex shapes. Limitations: anisotropy, delamination/impact damage, repair/recycling difficulty and temperature limits set by the matrix. Uses: aircraft/vehicle components, boat hulls, sports goods, chemical tanks/pipes, wind-turbine components and structural strengthening. No universal claim that every FRP is stronger/cheaper than every metal is justified.

smp.title: Shape-memory polymers
paragraphs: A shape-memory polymer (SMP) can be programmed into a temporary shape and recover a permanent shape when stimulated. Permanent netpoints/cross-links preserve the reference shape; switching segments fix and release the temporary shape through a transition such as glass transition or melting.

Thermal cycle: heat above the switching transition, deform to a temporary shape, cool under constraint to fix it, then remove the constraint. Reheat to activate segmental mobility and recover the permanent shape. Unlike ordinary plastic deformation, the temporary deformation is deliberately recoverable.

Other activation routes include light-responsive chemistry, electrical/Joule heating with conducting fillers, magnetic heating of embedded particles and water-induced plasticisation. Electrical/magnetic activation may act through heat rather than a direct shape-changing field effect.

Features: lightweight, large programmable deformation, tunable switching temperature and flexible manufacture. Applications: actuators, self-deploying structures, seals, responsive textiles, robotics, catheters/stents and drug-delivery/scaffold research. Biocompatibility and biodegradability depend on the particular polymer and are not properties of all SMPs.

pla.title: Biodegradable polymers and PLA
paragraphs: Biodegradable polymers break down through biological activity under suitable conditions. They can reduce persistent waste where appropriate collection/treatment is available, and allow temporary biomedical devices that gradually resorb. Biodegradable does not mean instant, harmless degradation in every environment.

PLA (polylactic acid) is an aliphatic polyester with repeating unit [–O–CH(CH₃)–CO–]ₙ. Ferment carbohydrate feedstocks to lactic acid, then form polymer by polycondensation (removing water) or convert to lactide and use ring-opening polymerisation. It is a thermoplastic; bio-based origin and biodegradability are separate classifications.

Features include renewable feedstock, transparency, useful stiffness and processing by extrusion/moulding/3D printing. Limitations include brittleness, heat resistance and slow breakdown in ordinary soil/marine environments. Industrial composting conditions are usually important. Uses: packaging/films/cups, fibres and 3D-printing filament, and suitable medical grades for sutures, drug delivery and tissue scaffolds.

corrosion.title: Electrochemical corrosion and rusting of iron
paragraphs: Corrosion is deterioration of a material by reaction with its environment. Effects include loss of metal/strength, leakage and equipment failure, contamination, poor appearance and replacement/maintenance costs. Dry corrosion is direct chemical attack (often gas/metal reaction at elevated temperature); wet corrosion involves anodic/cathodic reactions connected through a metal and an electrolyte.

For iron in aerated neutral water: anode Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻; cathode O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Ferrous ions form Fe(OH)₂: Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂. Further oxidation: 4Fe(OH)₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃. Subsequent dehydration/ageing gives hydrated ferric oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (rust). The porous rust is not an effective continuous barrier.

In deaerated acidic solution, cathodic hydrogen evolution can occur: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. For iron, combine this with Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ to obtain Fe + 2H⁺ → Fe²⁺ + H₂. State the environment when choosing the cathodic reaction; do not add both cathodic reactions indiscriminately.

galvanic.title: Galvanic and differential-aeration corrosion
paragraphs: Galvanic (differential-metal) corrosion occurs when dissimilar metals are electrically connected in an electrolyte. The more active member becomes the anode and dissolves; the more noble member supports cathodic reduction. For a steel–copper connection in typical aerated water, steel is anodic: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻, while oxygen reduction occurs preferentially on copper. Use compatible metals, electrical isolation and suitable coatings to reduce attack. Nuts and bolts of the same metal avoid creating such a couple.

Differential-aeration corrosion can occur on one metal where oxygen access differs. The oxygen-poor region becomes anodic relative to the oxygen-rich region. Under a water drop, the centre is less aerated and iron dissolves there; the rim supports oxygen reduction. In a partly filled tank, attack is concentrated just below the waterline because that region is less oxygenated than the near-surface cathodic area.

Pitting begins at local passive-film breakdown/occluded regions. A small active pit is coupled to a large surrounding cathodic surface, concentrating anodic current. Restricted transport and chloride-rich acidic conditions can sustain the pit. Chloride solution also increases electrolyte conductivity and can disrupt passive films; not every salt affects every metal equally.

factors.title: Factors controlling corrosion
paragraphs: Metal factors: position in the relevant galvanic series/electrode tendency, purity, passive film, oxide-film character, stress and relative anode/cathode area. Environmental factors: moisture, oxygen distribution, pH, dissolved salts/conductivity, temperature and corrosive gases. The actual environment and kinetics matter; a standard-potential ranking alone cannot predict every rate.

Impurities may form microgalvanic cathodes, so impure zinc commonly corrodes faster than pure zinc in the same salt solution. A small anode connected to a large cathode suffers high anodic current density (current/anode area), causing intense local attack. A large anode/small cathode is usually less severe per unit anodic area.

Passivity is formation of a thin, adherent protective film. Aluminium can resist corrosion despite its active position because Al₂O₃ limits further attack, while ordinary iron rust is porous. Higher temperature commonly accelerates reactions/diffusion, but dissolved-oxygen changes and film formation can alter the trend. Acidic pH often accelerates dissolution/hydrogen evolution; amphoteric metals may also be attacked in strong alkali.

Pilling–Bedworth ratio = volume of oxide formed / volume of metal consumed. Ratios below one often imply incomplete coverage; moderately above one may favour a continuous film; very large ratios can cause stresses/cracking. This is a useful oxide-film guideline, not a universal quantitative corrosion-rate law; adhesion, defects, volatility and service conditions also matter.

protection.title: Cathodic protection
paragraphs: Cathodic protection suppresses metal dissolution by making the structure the cathode. In the sacrificial-anode method, connect a more active metal such as Mg, Zn or a suitable Al alloy to the steel in the electrolyte. The sacrificial metal oxidises (for example Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) and supplies electrons to the steel. Inspect and replace consumed anodes. No external DC supply is needed, but available driving voltage/current is limited.

In impressed-current protection, connect the structure to the negative terminal of a DC source and a suitable auxiliary anode to its positive terminal. Current passes through the electrolyte from the auxiliary anode to the structure; the structure is polarised cathodically. It suits large pipelines, tanks and marine structures, with controllable output. It requires power, monitoring and care against overprotection/interference.

Sacrificial anodes are consumable and simpler for suitably sized systems; impressed-current systems can protect larger/high-current-demand structures but need a maintained power/control installation. Neither method works merely by calling the metal a cathode: an adequate electrical path, electrolyte and protective current are required.

coatings.title: Galvanising, tinning and food-contact cautions
paragraphs: Galvanising coats iron/steel with zinc. Intact zinc is a barrier; if scratched in a suitable electrolyte, zinc remains more active and dissolves sacrificially, protecting exposed iron. Tinning coats with tin, a more noble metal: intact tin is a barrier, but a scratch can create an iron-anode/tin-cathode couple and accelerate local steel attack. Thus galvanising offers sacrificial protection after small coating damage, unlike ordinary tinning.

Galvanising is a surface-coating method that can also give sacrificial cathodic protection. Separate-anode cathodic protection supplies protective current without requiring the whole structure to be zinc-coated. These are related principles, not mutually exclusive phenomena.

The traditional reason for tinning brass utensils is to separate food from copper/zinc-containing brass. Zinc coatings can dissolve in acidic foods and contaminate them, so galvanised vessels are unsuitable for acidic food storage/cooking. Tin linings must be intact and appropriate for food use; no blanket claim of safety for every food, temperature or damaged lining is justified.

spectroscopy.title: Spectroscopy and Beer–Lambert law
paragraphs: Spectroscopy studies interactions of electromagnetic radiation with matter. In UV–visible absorption spectroscopy, suitable photons promote electrons to higher electronic energy levels. A chromophore is the atom/group responsible for characteristic absorption, for example a conjugated dye group. λmax is the wavelength at which an absorption band has its maximum absorbance under the stated conditions.

The conventional UV range is about 200–400 nm for routine solution instruments (the wider UV region extends below 200 nm); visible light is about 400–700 nm, sometimes extended to 800 nm by convention. State the convention rather than treating the boundary as exact.

Beer–Lambert law: A = log₁₀(I₀/I) = εlc, where A is dimensionless absorbance, ε is molar absorptivity (L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹), l is optical path length (cm) and c is concentration (mol L⁻¹). It assumes suitable monochromatic light and a homogeneous, non-scattering solution within its linear concentration range. Chemical changes, stray light and turbidity can cause deviations.

dye.title: Dye-effluent analysis by UV–visible spectroscopy
paragraphs: A coloured dye such as methylene blue absorbs at a characteristic visible wavelength through electronic transitions. Use a solvent/reagent blank, scan a representative standard and select λmax (methylene blue is commonly measured near 664 nm in dilute water, but determine the actual maximum for the sample conditions).

Prepare several known standards covering the expected range. Measure their absorbances with the same cuvette/path length, blank-correct them and plot A against concentration. Fit A = mc + b over the verified linear range. Filter/clarify a turbid sample when appropriate without removing the analyte; dilute if needed. Measure the sample under identical conditions.

Calculate c_diluted = (A_sample − b)/m, then c_original = dilution factor × c_diluted. Report units, dilution and calibration range. For treatment studies, removal % = [(c_initial − c_final)/c_initial]×100, comparing consistent volume/basis. No numeric concentration can be obtained without measured absorbance and calibration/ε.

This supports monitoring dye effluents, treatment efficiency and discharge trends. Mixed dyes, pH changes and suspended particles may interfere; a single dye absorbance is not a universal measure of total organic pollution or COD. ir.title: IR principle, night vision and CO monitoring
paragraphs: IR absorption occurs when radiation matches a molecular vibrational transition that changes the molecular dipole moment. The fundamental mid-IR region is commonly about 4000–400 cm⁻¹. CO has an IR-active stretching vibration (near 4.6–4.7 μm), allowing selective optical detection.

Active IR systems supply illumination and detect its reflection, transmission or absorption. Passive IR systems detect radiation emitted by objects without an illumination beam. Thermal night-vision cameras map emitted IR into an image; passive motion/security detectors sense changes in received thermal radiation. Active near-IR night-vision systems instead use an illuminator and reflected light.

A typical non-dispersive IR (NDIR) CO analyser is active: IR source → gas sample cell → wavelength-selective filter/detector, with a reference measurement and electronics. CO absorbs at its characteristic band, reducing transmitted intensity. Calibration relates absorbance/signal ratio to CO concentration; reference channels compensate source drift and non-specific effects.

In a PUC application, take a representative exhaust sample, manage particulates/condensation as required, zero/span-calibrate the analyser, measure the CO-specific signal, and report calibrated CO concentration (often volume %). Compare with the applicable vehicle/test limit; no limit can be invented without the regulation/category.

Source correction: describing an analyser with its own IR source as “passive” is inconsistent. CO sensing by absorption is not the same as a passive thermal motion detector. Night vision is also an imaging/detection application of IR, not necessarily a molecular spectrometer.

raman.title: Raman effect and tumour investigation
paragraphs: The Raman effect is inelastic scattering of light: the molecule exchanges energy with the photon so the scattered frequency differs from the incident frequency. Rayleigh scattering has no frequency shift; Stokes photons lose energy and anti-Stokes photons gain energy. Raman-active vibrations change molecular polarisability. The Raman shift is commonly expressed in cm⁻¹.

A laser illuminates the sample; collection optics gather scattered light, filters suppress intense Rayleigh light, and a spectrograph/detector records the Raman spectrum. Bands provide molecular fingerprints, supporting material identification, reaction monitoring and biomedical studies.

Healthy and tumour tissue can differ in proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. Acquire spectra from tissue/biopsy locations, subtract background/fluorescence carefully, normalise and compare with validated reference spectra. Statistical classification (for example PCA followed by a suitable validated classifier) can distinguish patterns and map candidate tumour boundaries.

Benefits include molecular specificity, potentially limited sample preparation and suitability for spatial mapping. Limitations include weak signals, fluorescence, tissue heterogeneity, laser heating and validation requirements. No single universal peak or protein/lipid ratio proves cancer. The supplied example is supporting diagnostic evidence, not a replacement for validated clinical assessment/histopathology; the packet’s repeated lung example labelled as prostate is not treated as prostate-specific evidence.

nitinol.title: Nitinol and the shape-memory effect
paragraphs: Nitinol is a near-equiatomic nickel–titanium alloy named from Nickel–Titanium–Naval Ordnance Laboratory. Its reversible solid-state transformation is between high-temperature austenite and low-temperature martensite; it is a phase/structure change, not melting. Austenite is commonly described by the ordered cubic B2 structure and martensite by a lower-symmetry, commonly monoclinic B19′ structure.

Shape-memory cycle: establish the permanent shape in austenite; cool to twinned martensite; deform at low temperature by variant reorientation/detwinning; heat through the reverse-transformation range so austenite reforms and the original shape returns. Cooling alone does not necessarily produce the temporary deformed shape again in a one-way alloy.

Superelasticity is different: above the appropriate transformation temperature, applied stress induces martensite; removal of stress allows transformation back to austenite and large recoverable strain without a heating step. Transformation temperatures and recoverable strain depend on composition, processing and load.

Features: shape recovery, superelasticity, useful corrosion resistance, high damping and high strength relative to useful device size. Applications include orthodontic wires, stents, guidewires, actuators, couplings and flexible spectacle frames. Biocompatibility depends on alloy surface/device design and patient factors, not an unconditional nickel-safety claim.

stm.title: Scanning tunnelling microscopy
paragraphs: STM maps suitable electrically conducting surfaces using quantum tunnelling. Bring a sharp conducting tip (commonly tungsten or platinum–iridium) within a very small gap of the conducting sample and apply bias. A tunnelling current flows without ordinary mechanical contact. Sharpness, conductivity and mechanical stability make W/Pt–Ir useful; the tip material alone does not guarantee atomic resolution.

Components: tip, bias/current-measurement circuit, x–y–z piezoelectric scanner, coarse approach, feedback controller/computer and vibration isolation. At comparable bias/electronic conditions the current decreases approximately exponentially with gap: I ∝ exp(−2κs), not directly in proportion to distance. Electronic density of states also affects the signal.

Constant-current mode: feedback adjusts z to hold a selected current while scanning x–y; record z(x,y). Constant-height mode: hold nominal tip height, record current variations; use sufficiently flat samples to avoid collisions. Fixed height is not a fixed local gap on an uneven surface.

Applications: atomic-scale surface features, defects, adsorbates, semiconductor surfaces, electronic-state studies and controlled atom manipulation. Limitations: conductive path required, sensitivity to drift/vibration/tip condition, small scan areas and specialised operation. STM does not require exactly 0 K and is not a literal optical photograph of atoms. Source correction: the DOCX’s direct current–distance proportionality is wrong.

afm.title: Atomic force microscopy
paragraphs: AFM measures tip–sample interactions using a sharp tip on a flexible cantilever. A piezo scanner moves the tip/sample across the surface; a laser reflected from the cantilever onto a position-sensitive detector senses bending/oscillation. Feedback maintains the chosen interaction setpoint and records surface height. In a calibrated small-deflection description, force F = kδ, where k is cantilever spring constant and δ its deflection.

Contact mode keeps continuous contact and can cause lateral-force damage. Non-contact mode monitors changes in an oscillating cantilever above the surface. Tapping mode makes intermittent contact, often reducing lateral damage to soft samples. Calibration and mode choice affect the interpretation.

Uses: surface topography/roughness, polymer/ceramic/biological imaging, adhesion, friction and mechanical-property mapping. AFM can investigate insulating as well as conducting samples and can operate in air, liquids or vacuum with suitable equipment. Limitations include tip-convolution effects, possible damage, drift, small scan area and slow scans.

Comparison: STM measures tunnelling current with a conducting tip/sample circuit, in constant-current or constant-height modes; AFM measures mechanical interactions with a cantilever in contact/non-contact/tapping modes. Both use fine scanning and feedback. Neither has universally better resolution/speed in every setting; compare a specified instrument, sample and mode. Conflicting numerical scan limits in the notes are not universal specifications.

healing.title: Self-healing materials
paragraphs: Self-healing materials restore some lost integrity/function after damage through a built-in repair mechanism. Repair can be autonomic (damage triggers it) or externally activated (for example heat/light). It is not necessarily complete, unlimited or intervention-free.

Extrinsic capsule systems embed healing agent in microcapsules. A crack ruptures capsules, agent flows into the crack and reacts/polymerises, sometimes with an embedded catalyst. Vascular systems deliver agent through channels; replenishment can permit repeated repair. A depleted one-use capsule cannot heal indefinitely.

Intrinsic systems rely on reversible bonds/interactions or molecular mobility within the material, for example reversible Diels–Alder bonds or hydrogen-bond networks. Heating or another suitable stimulus allows damaged interfaces to reconnect; cooling/rebonding restores useful properties. Intrinsic/extrinsic and autonomic/non-autonomic describe different classification axes.

Applications: anticorrosion/scratch-resistant coatings, aircraft/vehicle composites, concrete systems, sealants, adhesives, pipelines and cables. Benefits include extended service life and lower maintenance; recovery depends on crack size, environment, agent supply and mechanical requirements. No source product lifetime is a universal guarantee.

biosensor.title: Biosensors and amperometric glucose monitoring
paragraphs: A biosensor combines a biological recognition element with a transducer and signal processing. Recognition elements include enzymes, antibodies, nucleic acids and cells. The recognition element selects/interacts with analyte; the transducer converts this change to a measurable signal; electronics amplify/process and display the calibrated result.

By transduction: electrochemical (amperometric current, potentiometric potential, conductometric conductivity), optical, thermal and piezoelectric/mass-sensitive. Useful features are selectivity, sensitivity, reproducibility, suitable response time/range, stable immobilisation and calibration, low interference and appropriate cost/size. Implantable designs also require appropriate biocompatibility.

Glucose example: immobilise glucose oxidase (GOx) near the working electrode, use a reference electrode and where required a counter electrode, and hold a suitable potential. GOx catalyses glucose + O₂ → gluconolactone + H₂O₂; gluconolactone + H₂O → gluconic acid. At an oxidation-detection electrode: H₂O₂ → O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻. The measured current is related by calibration to glucose over the usable range.

Overall acid-forming enzyme reaction: C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₇ + H₂O₂. Water is essential to balance the net reaction; the DOCX omits it. Interfering oxidisable species, oxygen availability, enzyme ageing, temperature and fouling need control. Mediated and other commercial glucose sensors may use different electron-transfer schemes.

Applications include blood-glucose meters, appropriately designed continuous monitors, food/fermentation analysis and environmental sensing. Biosensing materials include immobilised GOx on a suitable conductive support; a support alone is not the biological recognition element. Benefits include selective, rapid and potentially portable analysis, subject to calibration and device-specific limitations.

nano.title: Nanomaterials and synthesis
paragraphs: Nanomaterials have at least one relevant structural dimension approximately 1–100 nm. Their high surface-area/volume ratio and size-dependent structure can change optical, electrical, mechanical and catalytic properties compared with bulk material.

Top-down synthesis reduces bulk material: mechanical/ball milling, lithography or suitable etching/ablation. It can suit patterned manufacture but may introduce defects, contamination and size-distribution limits. Bottom-up synthesis builds from atoms/molecules: precipitation, sol–gel, chemical vapour deposition or self-assembly. It permits compositional/size control under suitable conditions but requires control of nucleation, growth and aggregation.

In sol–gel synthesis, hydrolyse a suitable precursor, condense it into a sol/network, allow gelation, then dry and heat/treat as needed for the target oxide. Milling instead repeatedly fractures/deforms particles mechanically. Select the route for the material; no single method produces every nanomaterial. STM and AFM characterise appropriate surfaces rather than being general synthesis methods.

biochip.title: Biochips
paragraphs: A biochip is a miniaturised platform that performs biological/biochemical measurements, often with many tests in parallel. Examples include DNA microarrays, protein arrays and microfluidic lab-on-chip devices. A biochip is not necessarily an implanted identity device.

Advantages include small reagent/sample volumes, parallel/high-throughput analysis, potential automation, compact size and rapid assays. Limitations include fabrication/calibration costs, cross-reactivity, sample preparation and the need to validate the particular assay. Applications: gene-expression/genetic testing, pathogen detection, drug screening, biomarker research and point-of-care testing.

lubricants.title: Lubricants: functions and classes
paragraphs: A lubricant is introduced between moving surfaces to reduce friction and wear. It can also remove heat, seal, protect against corrosion, carry debris and damp noise. Liquids include mineral oils, fatty oils and synthetic oils (for example silicones/esters); semisolids include greases; solids include graphite, molybdenum disulphide (MoS₂) and PTFE.

Grease is lubricating oil thickened by a soap or another thickener. Traditional soap types include calcium, sodium and lithium greases; their water/temperature properties differ. Consistency describes resistance to deformation/penetration and affects retention and flow. Dropping point is the specified test temperature at which a drop separates; it is not automatically a maximum safe operating temperature.

Synthetic lubricants can offer more controlled composition, oxidation/thermal stability and low-temperature behaviour than conventional mineral oils, but superiority depends on formulation and compatibility. Blended oils mix base oils and/or additives: antioxidants (for example hindered phenols), corrosion inhibitors, antiwear/EP additives, detergents/dispersants, viscosity-index improvers, pour-point depressants and antifoams. Antioxidants suppress oxidation-chain reactions and sludge/acid formation.

Space/vacuum applications often use suitable low-volatility solid lubricants such as MoS₂ (or specialised fluids selected for the environment). Graphite depends strongly on environment and is not a universal vacuum substitute. There is no single fixed “space lubricant composition” without a specified device; the source’s MoS₂ example should be stated as an example, not an industry-wide recipe.

lubrication.title: Lubrication mechanisms and operating conditions
paragraphs: Hydrodynamic/thick-film lubrication: a continuous viscous oil film separates surfaces; motion and geometry develop load-carrying pressure. Low friction results mainly from shearing fluid, not metal contact. It suits adequate speed and appropriate load/viscosity; a suitable mineral or synthetic oil can be used. The supplied course examples classify watches, clocks and sewing machines under fluid-film lubrication; use that stated course classification while recognising that a real instrument’s lubrication regime depends on its load, speed and geometry.

Boundary/thin-film lubrication: at low speed, high load or startup, a full hydrodynamic film may not form. Polar molecules/antiwear additives adsorb or react on surfaces to provide a protective thin layer. Fatty oils/blends or formulated oils can provide boundary lubricity. Heavy loads and slow speeds commonly require this mechanism; delicate low-load instruments may use low-viscosity oils, with the actual regime determined by speed/load/clearance.

Extreme-pressure (EP) lubrication: severe loads/sliding heat can break down ordinary boundary films. Sulphur-, phosphorus- or other suitable additives react at hot contact points to form protective low-shear films that reduce welding/seizure. Hypoid gears and severe metal-forming/wire-drawing contacts may require EP formulations.

Source qualification: “transformer lubrication” is imprecise—transformer oil primarily insulates electrically and removes heat, not lubricates a moving contact. Gold/platinum and other very inert surfaces may not form the intended reactive EP layer; some sulphur additives instead corrode copper-containing metals. Thus “metals resistant to EP lubrication” has no universal list independent of additive chemistry and temperature.

oilproperties.title: Lubricant properties and oil selection
paragraphs: Viscosity measures resistance to flow at a specified temperature. Viscosity index describes how strongly viscosity changes with temperature: high VI means relatively less change. A very viscous oil can still have a low VI, so viscosity and VI are not interchangeable.

Cloud point is the specified cooling-test temperature at which wax/cloudiness first appears; pour point is the lowest specified-test temperature at which flow is observed. Low values matter for cold-weather operation and pumpability. Flash point is the lowest specified-test temperature at which vapour momentarily ignites; fire point is the temperature at which combustion is sustained under the test conditions. Adequately high flash/fire points reduce fire risk at operating temperature, but do not alone prove lubrication quality or safety.

Redwood viscometers measure the time for a fixed volume (traditionally 50 mL) to flow through a calibrated orifice at a controlled temperature. No. 1 has a smaller orifice for lower/medium-viscosity oils; No. 2 has a larger orifice for more viscous oils so the outflow time remains practical. Report temperature and instrument number with the time; Redwood seconds are not themselves SI dynamic-viscosity units.

Transformer oils require high dielectric strength, oxidation stability, suitable low-temperature flow and low moisture/impurities. Refrigeration compressor oils must be compatible with the refrigerant and compressor, with suitable viscosity, low-temperature properties and chemical stability; the suitable mineral/synthetic oil depends on the refrigerant. One oil cannot be specified for every refrigeration system.

smart.title: Smart materials
paragraphs: Smart materials respond to a stimulus such as temperature, stress, electric/magnetic field, light or chemical environment with a useful change in a property. Examples include Nitinol shape-memory alloy, shape-memory polymers, piezoelectric ceramics and photochromic materials. Their response can be designed for sensing, actuation or adaptation; not every smart material has all these responses.

caustic.title: Caustic embrittlement and boiler corrosion
paragraphs: Caustic embrittlement is intergranular cracking of stressed boiler steel associated with concentrated caustic alkali. Sodium carbonate can produce alkaline conditions: Na₂CO₃ + H₂O ⇌ NaHCO₃ + NaOH. Concentration by evaporation in crevices/riveted joints can create aggressive conditions at stressed regions; hydrogen/stress effects depend on the service conditions.

The traditional course net scheme is Na₂CO₃ + H₂O → 2NaOH + CO₂ under the described boiler conditions. The aqueous carbonate hydrolysis step can instead be written Na₂CO₃ + H₂O ⇌ NaHCO₃ + NaOH. Both descriptions explain the development of caustic alkalinity; the net scheme is a simplified course model, not an unrestricted ambient-water conversion.

Prevention in the supplied textbook (printed p.10): use sodium phosphate rather than sodium carbonate; tannin/lignin or sodium sulphate are described as blocking hair-cracks and reducing caustic penetration. This is the course explanation for why Na₂SO₄ controls caustic embrittlement; it is not neutralisation of NaOH. The text gives historical Na₂SO₄:NaOH concentration ratios of 1:1, 2:1 and 3:1 for its stated pressure categories. Actual boiler dosing must follow the applicable engineered water-chemistry programme, rather than using those textbook ratios as a universal operating instruction.

Dissolved O₂ accelerates corrosion/pitting; remove it by deaeration and suitable scavengers: 2Na₂SO₃ + O₂ → 2Na₂SO₄, or N₂H₄ + O₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O (a historical toxic chemical requiring controlled handling). CO₂ dissolves to form carbonic acid: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃, increasing condensate-line corrosion; remove/neutralise it through properly designed treatment. Hydrolysis of MgCl₂ can create acidic corrosive conditions. Prevent corrosion through feedwater treatment, deaeration and monitored chemistry, not improvised chemical dosing.

energyextras.title: Conventional and alternative energy
paragraphs: Coal-fired power plants burn coal to heat boiler water into steam; steam drives a turbine coupled to a generator. Condensation and feedwater return complete the cycle. Useful coal requires suitable calorific value, low undesirable moisture/ash/sulphur and combustion properties matched to the plant.

Fossil fuels are finite, unevenly distributed and emit CO₂ and other pollutants. Diversification can improve supply security and reduce pollution. Non-conventional alternatives discussed in older course notes include solar, wind, biomass, geothermal, tidal and wave energy. Renewable does not mean impact-free.

Wind turbines convert moving-air energy into rotor mechanical energy and then generator output. Wind is fuel-free and low-emission during operation, but variable/site-dependent; grid integration, storage, land/ecology and noise require management. Biomass converts organic matter by combustion, digestion (biogas) or other processing. It can use wastes and be storable, but logistics, air emissions, land competition and sustainable regrowth matter; it is not automatically carbon-neutral.

Geothermal systems use underground heat, sometimes producing steam/hot fluid to drive turbines or supply heat. Benefits include firm output at suitable sites and low operating emissions; limitations include site dependence, drilling cost, corrosive fluids and possible induced seismicity.

The question about energy “due to decay of radioactive materials” needs precision: radioactive decay releases nuclear energy; radioisotope generators can convert decay heat into electricity for long-lived remote/space power. Ordinary nuclear power stations principally use controlled fission, not spontaneous decay alone. Advantages include high energy density and reliable output; radiation protection, waste and cost remain concerns. This distinction is a general-chemistry clarification of the question’s wording.

paragraphs: Useful battery features include suitable voltage and capacity, high energy/power density for its task, low self-discharge and good shelf life, safe operation, acceptable cost and temperature range, and reliable output. A secondary battery additionally needs useful cycle life and charge efficiency. Rechargeability is not a feature of every primary cell.

subpart_answers.title: Total carbon
subpart_answers.text: Total carbon includes carbon in fixed carbon and volatile constituents. It is measured in ultimate analysis and is distinct from proximate fixed carbon; a larger useful combustible-carbon fraction generally increases available heat.

subpart_answers.label: d

subpart_answers.label: a
subpart_answers.title: Passivity
subpart_answers.text: An adherent, continuous passive film restricts transport and further reaction, allowing active metals such as aluminium to resist corrosion in suitable environments. Film breakdown can reverse this protection.

subpart_answers.label: b
subpart_answers.title: Position of the metal
subpart_answers.text: In a dissimilar-metal couple in a specified electrolyte, the more active member is usually anodic and dissolves. The relevant galvanic series, film condition and polarisation matter; standard potentials alone do not fix every corrosion rate.

subpart_answers.label: c
subpart_answers.title: Relative areas
subpart_answers.text: A large cathode coupled to a small anode concentrates dissolution current on the small anodic area. High anodic current density produces intense local attack; avoid this area combination.

subpart_answers.label: d
subpart_answers.title: pH
subpart_answers.text: Acid often increases dissolution and permits cathodic H₂ evolution. Higher pH can favour protective hydroxide/oxide films, but amphoteric metals can also dissolve in strong alkali. The trend is metal- and environment-dependent.

subpart_answers.label: a
subpart_answers.title: Fluid-film / hydrodynamic lubrication
subpart_answers.text: Hydrodynamic/thick-film lubrication: a continuous viscous oil film separates surfaces; motion and geometry develop load-carrying pressure. Low friction results mainly from shearing fluid, not metal contact. It suits adequate speed and appropriate load/viscosity; a suitable mineral or synthetic oil can be used.

subpart_answers.label: b
subpart_answers.title: Boundary / thin-film lubrication
subpart_answers.text: Boundary/thin-film lubrication: at low speed, high load or startup, a full hydrodynamic film may not form. Polar molecules/antiwear additives adsorb or react on surfaces to provide a protective thin layer. Fatty oils/blends or formulated oils can provide boundary lubricity. Heavy loads and slow speeds commonly require this mechanism; delicate low-load instruments may use low-viscosity oils, with the actual regime determined by speed/load/clearance.

subpart_answers.label: c
subpart_answers.title: Extreme-pressure lubrication
subpart_answers.text: Extreme-pressure (EP) lubrication: severe loads/sliding heat can break down ordinary boundary films. Sulphur-, phosphorus- or other suitable additives react at hot contact points to form protective low-shear films that reduce welding/seizure. Hypoid gears and severe metal-forming/wire-drawing contacts may require EP formulations.

subpart_answers.title: Cloud point
subpart_answers.text: The specified cooling-test temperature where wax/cloudiness first appears; it helps judge cold-weather suitability.

subpart_answers.label: b
subpart_answers.title: Pour point
subpart_answers.text: The lowest specified-test temperature at which oil still flows. Select a suitably low pour point for the coldest expected service.

subpart_answers.label: c
subpart_answers.title: Flash point
subpart_answers.text: The lowest specified-test temperature where vapour flashes momentarily on applying an ignition source; it informs fire-risk assessment.

subpart_answers.label: d
subpart_answers.title: Fire point
subpart_answers.text: The lowest specified-test temperature for sustained burning under the stated test (traditionally at least five seconds). A suitably high value is desirable, but it is not the maximum operating temperature by itself.
